feed.title: New reports — Lunenburg Budget Project
feed.subtitle: Every report and page this project publishes, the day it first appears.

entry.title: School receipts to the Town
entry.summary: The schools brought in $183,945 in FY2025 that the Town books as general fund revenue, 3.1 times its plan.

entry.title: Salaries from grants and fees
entry.summary: Grants and fee funds paid $7,268,170 of school salaries in four years; no account names the job.

entry.title: Town general fund
entry.summary: The Town planned on $49,326,796 of general fund revenue for FY2026; 71.0% of it is the property tax levy.

entry.title: Preschool
entry.summary: Preschool tuition goes to the Town, not the schools; in FY2025 it brought in 4.2 times what the Town planned.

entry.title: Lunenburg Historical Report
entry.summary: Every annual town report this archive holds, read for what it says about the town across all of them: the tax rate and the revaluations beside its falls, the population, the longest names on the school rosters, and the road from the first study of a town manager to the charter. Each figure cites its edition and page.

entry.title: School lines against budget
entry.summary: School lines land near their vote in total every year, and far from it one by one, in both directions.

entry.title: After-school activities fund
entry.summary: The after-school activities fund spent $205,917 in FY2026. Trips were its largest use, then pay.

entry.title: Fee fund history
entry.summary: In FY2025 the town budget took $254,121 of the fee fund’s costs by journal entry, against $131,481 of fees.

entry.title: Athletic director
entry.summary: No record held pays the director from the fee fund. The FY2026 vote set his line $20,407 below level service.

entry.title: FY breakdown
entry.summary: The school lines left $32,022 in FY2023 and $482,118 in FY2026; pick a year to see what moved in it.

entry.title: Special education grants
entry.summary: Special education grants and the circuit breaker paid $1,055,922 in FY2023 and $773,361 in FY2026.

entry.title: Senior tax work-off
entry.summary: Seniors in the work-off fell from 16 in 2010 to 6 in 2025, while the cap rose from $750 to $1,500.

entry.title: Year-end tuition payment
entry.summary: On 30 June 2026 the school general fund paid $189,277 on FLLAC invoices numbered for FY2027.

entry.title: Circuit breaker and surplus
entry.summary: FY2026’s vote counted on $480,204 of circuit breaker for collaborative tuition; $333,495 came, on 29 June.

entry.title: Surprise costs
entry.summary: A surprise cost is spending above the budget as voted: $1,235,009 over 17 years.

entry.title: Grants for surprises
entry.summary: The circuit breaker paid a median $507,832 a year, FY2010 to FY2026; IDEA allocated $437,380 for FY2027.

entry.title: Reserve or budget
entry.summary: Budgeting the cushion every year raises $2,345,375 more than a reserve covering the same years.

entry.title: Reserve options
entry.summary: Seven ways to size the reserve run from $90,554 to $412,397; the law caps it at $541,717.

entry.title: Tuition after repayment
entry.summary: Of $230,514 a year for an average private placement, Lunenburg keeps $96,943 after the state repays $133,571.

entry.title: Move-ins
entry.summary: A child in a private placement who moves in is the former town’s cost that year; after 1 April, the next too.

entry.title: Special education reserve fund
entry.summary: A special education line spent past its vote in 13 of 17 years, on top of the state repayment the vote counts on. A median bad year of the last five ran $116,811 over; the worst year on record, $223,774. Held once, a reserve costs less than a yearly cushion.

entry.title: Positions and their funds
entry.summary: Of 10 general fund leadership accounts, 2 had any pay moved to or from another fund.

entry.title: Pay moved between funds
entry.summary: Journal entries moved $545,630 of general fund pay onto other funds in four years, and $617,530 back.

entry.title: Special education definition
entry.summary: Our rules now count what DESE’s documents count; DESE’s FY2024 report still counts $743,667 more.

entry.title: Unspent money by fund
entry.summary: Fees, lunch and the circuit breaker held $1,692,438 at the end of FY2023; by our count, $1,119,636 by FY2026.

entry.title: School grants and aid
entry.summary: In FY2025 Chapter 70 aid was $8,988,960 and every grant spent $1,196,194: general aid beside restricted money.

entry.title: Paid outside the general fund
entry.summary: Funds outside the voted budget spent $16,680,612 in four years: 13.4% of school spending in FY2026.

entry.title: Grants other districts get
entry.summary: Comparison districts won 19 competitive grants Lunenburg did not in FY2026–FY2027; it won 2.

entry.title: Grant spending by line
entry.summary: Grant spending on a voted budget line went from 5.1% in FY2023 to 2.3% in FY2026.

entry.title: Grant allocations compared
entry.summary: Lunenburg gets less IDEA per pupil than most comparable districts; Title I tracks its low-income share.

entry.title: Carried-over orders
entry.summary: The general fund carried at most $190,128 of open orders into a new year, and the budget went with them.

entry.title: Budget lines, all funds
entry.summary: In FY2026 other funds spent $4,024,956 beside the general fund; $2,408,319 of it sat on no budget line.

entry.title: The whole school budget
entry.summary: The voted school budget is the general fund. Every fund together spent $29,929,041 in FY2026, $3,641,567 more, and these pages show where it came from and which lines it paid.

entry.title: Turf field capital plans
entry.summary: The schools have put the field in every capital plan of theirs since FY2022; its year kept moving.

entry.title: Special education burndown
entry.summary: In FY2026 the circuit breaker paid $4,005 from July to May, then $333,495 in one June entry.

entry.title: Inflation and school costs
entry.summary: Most of the rise in school spending since FY2009 is inflation: $8.9 million of $10.6 million a year.

entry.title: Surplus suggestions
entry.summary: The surplus came from many small leftovers, year after year, not one line; these options follow from that.

entry.title: Repeat underspending
entry.summary: 6 budget areas came in under every year from FY2023 to FY2026; 11 of 20 did in both FY2025 and FY2026.

entry.title: Surplus by year
entry.summary: Printed, FY2026 left $144,999 less than FY2025; on one footing it is $72,827 less, on the other $91,768 more.

entry.title: Budget burndown
entry.summary: By the end of March FY2026 had 40.2% of its budget left, against 33.0% and 32.6% in FY2023 and FY2024.

entry.title: Upkeep surplus, every dollar
entry.summary: Building upkeep left $195,934 in FY2026: $75,660 on one account, the rest on 13 others.

entry.title: What upkeep buys
entry.summary: Most of building upkeep is steady work: $291,136 to $389,138 a year to payees paid year after year.

entry.title: Usual purchases skipped
entry.summary: 10 payees the schools used every year were paid under half as usual in FY2026; 5 got nothing.

entry.title: Upkeep leftover by account
entry.summary: Building upkeep left $195,934 in FY2026 on 14 accounts; each card shows what was paid, skipped and released.

entry.title: Upkeep budget and spending
entry.summary: Building upkeep’s budget rose 96% from FY2023 to FY2026; what it spent rose 42%.

entry.title: Contracted building services
entry.summary: Third-party building services left $75,660 in FY2026, after two years of spending past the budget.

entry.title: Building upkeep
entry.summary: Building upkeep’s budget nearly doubled in four years, $332,016 to $652,033, while spending grew 42%. These pages show what it buys, and where the difference sits.

entry.title: Special education providers
entry.summary: Three payees took 66.5% of special education vendor payments; Keystone was paid 4.3 times as much by FY2026.

entry.title: Special education, all funds
entry.summary: Special education spending passed its voted budget every year, and other funds paid the difference.

entry.title: Teachers on the scale
entry.summary: In calendar 2025, 56 of 90 teachers we matched were paid at least the master’s top step.

entry.title: Teacher pay compared
entry.summary: Of 5 FY2026 salary schedules compared, Lunenburg’s top step was lowest in the bachelor’s and master’s lanes.

entry.title: Spending by type over time
entry.summary: School spending, all funds, went from $19,446,453 in FY2009 to $30,031,242 in FY2025.

entry.title: Pay or headcount
entry.summary: FY2025 had 15.2 fewer teachers than FY2009, but each cost $36,331 more; the teachers line rose $2,887,749.

entry.title: Growth by spending type
entry.summary: Each against its own FY2009 cost: insurance and retirement grew 83%, paras 89%, teachers 39%, all 54%.

entry.title: Teachers and other staff
entry.summary: The state counted 105.1 teacher FTE and 78.5 paraprofessional and support FTE in FY2025.

entry.title: Spending per child enrolled
entry.summary: After inflation, spending per child went from $8,518 in FY1994 to $15,217 in FY2024; pupils fell 10.1%.

entry.title: Long-run school spending
entry.summary: After inflation, net school spending went from $14,974,588 in FY1994 to $24,043,452 in FY2024, 1.61 times.

entry.title: Growth side by side
entry.summary: FY2008 to FY2024: spending up 12.7% after inflation (61.3% as printed); pupils down 13.4%, teacher FTE 4.6%.

entry.title: FY2011 teacher reading
entry.summary: The state’s file reads 102.3 teacher FTE for FY2011: 18.1 below FY2010 and 12.1 below FY2012.

entry.title: Projected school gap
entry.summary: Run forward on our assumed rates, the schools are $932,664 short in FY2028 and $4,675,101 in FY2033.

entry.title: Long-run balance rate
entry.summary: To balance for good, school costs could grow 2.82% a year; our rates give 5.18% a year.

entry.title: Level service cost
entry.summary: Keeping the same schools costs $1,396,847 more in FY2028, by our estimate: $28,361,400 in all.

entry.title: Gap by cost line
entry.summary: Health insurance puts $261,240 into the FY2028 gap from 14.9% of the school budget (ours).

entry.title: FY2028 revenue increase
entry.summary: The schools’ share of new revenue in FY2028 is $856,448 by our estimate, against $1,396,847 of costs.

entry.title: Development needed
entry.summary: Growth alone would need $2,153,691 of new levy a year (ours); the best year on record added $630,220.

entry.title: Cost and revenue growth
entry.summary: Keeping today’s schools costs 5.18% more each year; revenue grows 3.22% a year in FY2028, then less.

entry.title: Chapter 70 needed
entry.summary: For state aid alone to hold the gap, Chapter 70 would grow 11.32% a year (ours); we assume 2.71% a year.

entry.title: All cuts combined
entry.summary: Every sport, club, lawful office line and most technology: $1,495,880 (ours), enough for FY2028 and FY2029.

entry.title: Funding sources compared
entry.summary: Monty Tech took in $43,131,000 in FY2024 and Lunenburg schools $31,051,000: $30,204 and $19,653 a pupil.

entry.title: What per pupil counts
entry.summary: Three official measures of school spending count different things; neither state one counts capital.

entry.title: Lunenburg per-pupil breakdown
entry.summary: Lunenburg’s $18,027 a pupil in FY2025, by what it paid for: insurance and grants are in it, capital is not.

entry.title: Monty Tech per pupil
entry.summary: Monty Tech spent $25,827 a pupil in FY2025: above the all-district median, below the vocational one.

entry.title: Monty Tech per-pupil breakdown
entry.summary: Monty Tech’s $25,827 a pupil in FY2025, by what it paid for: insurance and grants are in it, capital is not.

entry.title: Monty Tech rate scenario
entry.summary: At Monty Tech’s FY2025 rate a pupil, Lunenburg would have spent $12,993,957 more, by our arithmetic.

entry.title: Monty Tech finances
entry.summary: Monty Tech is the regional vocational high school Lunenburg belongs to. Lunenburg’s bill was $1,334,521, most of it a minimum the state sets; the school spent $25,827 a pupil in FY2025, less than most vocational districts.

entry.title: Regional school share
entry.summary: Monty Tech’s FY2026 assessment was 3.80% of Lunenburg’s levy: about $283 of the average bill, our estimate.

entry.title: Home value and bill
entry.summary: A $500,000 home is taxed $7,195 a year in Lunenburg, 5th-highest of 15 nearby; in Leominster, $6,830.

entry.title: Harvard rate scenario
entry.summary: At Harvard’s FY2025 rate a pupil, Lunenburg would have spent $12,557,492 more, by our arithmetic.

entry.title: Harvard per pupil
entry.summary: Harvard spent $25,565 a pupil in FY2025, $7,538 more than Lunenburg, on DESE’s all-funds measure.

entry.title: Harvard per-pupil breakdown
entry.summary: Harvard’s $25,565 a pupil in FY2025 by what it bought: teachers first, 24.0% paid by grants and revolving.

entry.title: Harvard and Bromfield
entry.summary: Harvard, the district The Bromfield School belongs to, spent $25,565 a pupil in FY2025, $7,538 more than Lunenburg, on the same state measure. It serves a smaller low-income share, and nothing here shows the spending causes results.

entry.title: School revolving funds
entry.summary: The 9 school revolving funds took in $1,031,126 and paid out $1,119,195 in nine months of FY2026.

entry.title: School grant balances
entry.summary: 13 of the 46 school grant funds were overdrawn at 31 March 2026, by $378,942 together.

entry.title: School Committee funds
entry.summary: The schools held $1,592,572 in 61 funds outside the appropriation at 31 March 2026.

entry.title: Revolving fund history
entry.summary: The 9 school revolving funds closed FY2023 holding $1,074,431, against $306,471 at the close of FY2011.

entry.title: Monty Tech funding
entry.summary: State Chapter 70 aid paid 54.2% of Monty Tech’s FY2026 operating budget; the member towns paid 38.0%.

entry.title: Free cash
entry.summary: The state certified $3,354,370 of free cash as of 1 July 2025, the most the Town’s records list; 66.1% of the free cash identified that year was money appropriated and not spent.

entry.title: High school spending
entry.summary: Monty Tech spent $26,407 a pupil in FY2025 and Lunenburg High $19,644, on one DESE measure.

entry.title: High school enrolment
entry.summary: Lunenburg’s grades 9–12 fell 30.0% from FY2008 to FY2026; Monty Tech, all grades 9–12, rose 6.0%.

entry.title: Unpriced school charges
entry.summary: Nine charges a Lunenburg family can meet have no published amount anywhere in this archive.

entry.title: Reduced and waived fees
entry.summary: Three high schoolers at one sport each: $812.50 a year at the full fee, $150 reduced, $0 waived.

entry.title: Family fees
entry.summary: Two high schoolers, one sport each, the bus and a club: $978.75 in FY2026.

entry.title: Total state aid
entry.summary: The state’s cherry sheet carries $11,244,422 for Lunenburg for FY2026; Chapter 70 is 82.1% of it.

entry.title: State aid growth
entry.summary: Our projection grows all state aid 2.71% a year; the cherry sheet’s median yearly rise was 2.80%.

entry.title: Required local contribution
entry.summary: What the state requires the town to put in rose 37.8% from FY2019 to FY2026; Chapter 70 rose 22.4%.

entry.title: Spending against the median
entry.summary: In FY2024 Lunenburg ranked 238 of 362 districts on spending against its minimum; in FY2018 it was 181 of 361.

entry.title: Net school spending
entry.summary: Lunenburg spent 116.0% of the state’s minimum in FY2024, and met the minimum in all 31 years.

entry.title: Minimum aid
entry.summary: All of FY2026’s $240,450 increase was the Legislature’s minimum: $150 for each of 1,603 pupils.

entry.title: Foundation budget
entry.summary: The state priced Lunenburg’s schools at $22,073,946 for FY2026; Chapter 70 equals 41.8% of that.

entry.title: Cherry sheet variance
entry.summary: Cherry sheet receipts came in $390,814 short of the estimate in 2024 and $327,281 over in 2023.

entry.title: Cherry sheet assessments
entry.summary: The cherry sheet charged Lunenburg $1,003,251 for FY2026; 80.3% was tuition for pupils schooled elsewhere.

entry.title: Share of the school budget
entry.summary: Chapter 70 was 35.1% of the FY2026 school appropriation; the School Committee said 35%.

entry.title: Chapter 70 by year
entry.summary: Chapter 70 was $9,229,410 in FY2026 and $3,921,700 in FY2007; it fell in 2 of 19 years.

entry.title: Aid per pupil
entry.summary: Chapter 70 averaged $5,757.59 a pupil in FY2026, yet one pupil more or fewer moved it by $150.00.

entry.title: Chapter 70 aid
entry.summary: Chapter 70 was $9,229,410 of the $11,244,422 the state’s cherry sheet gave Lunenburg for FY2026. All of that year’s rise was the Legislature’s $150-a-pupil minimum; the formula itself added $0.

entry.title: Teachers per pupil
entry.summary: Lunenburg had 6.70 teacher FTE per hundred pupils in FY2025, 12th of 13 on the state’s sheet.

entry.title: Teachers by subject
entry.summary: From FY2024 to FY2026 subjects lost 12.3 teacher FTE and gained 2.2; science alone fell 4.2.

entry.title: Teachers by school
entry.summary: Turkey Hill Elementary went from 27.0 to 18.4 teacher FTE, FY2017 to FY2026; the district fell 8.7.

entry.title: Teachers over time
entry.summary: The state counted 103.4 teacher FTE in FY2026, 10.6 fewer than in FY2024; 95 of 171 year pairs end lower.

entry.title: Staff retention
entry.summary: The state reports 58.3% of paraprofessionals retained in FY2022 and 66.1% in FY2023, against 93.0% in FY2021.

entry.title: Staff by programme
entry.summary: Paraprofessional FTE coded to special education fell from 44.0 to 20.0 while the all-programmes count rose.

entry.title: Support staff
entry.summary: The town printed 7 counsellors, 3 psychologists and 2 social workers on its FY2025 school rosters.

entry.title: Printed school rosters
entry.summary: The town printed 250 names on its school rosters in FY2025, against 194 in FY2011.

entry.title: Paraprofessionals over time
entry.summary: The state counted 67.0 paraprofessional FTE in FY2025, against 14.8 in FY2013 and 46.4 in FY2009.

entry.title: Paraprofessional counts compared
entry.summary: For FY2025 the state counts 67.0 paraprofessional FTE; the town printed 52 paraprofessional names.

entry.title: People and posts
entry.summary: The state counted 123 teachers in FY2023, holding 112.8 full-time equivalent posts between them.

entry.title: District staff directory
entry.summary: The district’s staff directory listed 257 people on 30 October 2026; it carries no FTE and no fund.

entry.title: School staff
entry.summary: The state counted 103.4 teacher FTE in FY2026; whether that is a rise or a fall depends on the year it is measured from. Paraprofessional FTE was 67.0 in FY2025, the most per pupil on the state’s sheet. Nothing published says which posts were filled.

entry.title: Spending by function
entry.summary: Lunenburg was in the state’s bottom quarter on 7 of 10 DESE spending categories in FY2025.

entry.title: Spending and pupils
entry.summary: From FY2012 to FY2025 Lunenburg’s spending rose 48.7% and its pupils fell 5.6%; North Middlesex lost 23.5%.

entry.title: Regional districts
entry.summary: Nearby academic regional districts spent $18,142 to $22,664 a pupil in FY2025; Lunenburg spent $18,027.

entry.title: Spending per pupil
entry.summary: Lunenburg spent $18,027 a pupil in FY2025, all funds, against a state median of $23,520.

entry.title: Grants and revolving funds
entry.summary: Of $30,031,242 DESE counts for FY2025, grants and revolving funds paid $3,044,898: 10.1%.

entry.title: Gap by function
entry.summary: In-district, Lunenburg spent $2,103 a pupil less than Ayer Shirley, the middle of the six this project chose.

entry.title: Destination districts
entry.summary: 145 of the 177 children schooled elsewhere in FY2026 went to districts that spend more a pupil.

entry.title: Reaching the state median
entry.summary: At the FY2025 state median a pupil, Lunenburg would have spent $39,181,968, by our arithmetic.

entry.title: Comparison districts
entry.summary: Of six districts this project chose to compare, Lunenburg spent the least a pupil in FY2025.

entry.title: Average teacher salary
entry.summary: Lunenburg’s average teacher salary was $97,233 in FY2025, 2nd of the six districts this project compares.

entry.title: Spending compared
entry.summary: Lunenburg spent $18,027 a pupil in FY2025, all funds, against a state median of $23,520, and has sat in the state’s bottom quarter for 17 years. Its school general fund spent under its revised budget every year from FY2010 to FY2026.

entry.title: World languages
entry.summary: 57.8% of Lunenburg High took a language in SY2025, against 70.1% in SY2017; the middle school fell further.

entry.title: Override cut lists
entry.summary: The May 2024 override took 13 posts off the cut list; the 9 left match posts listed as cut for loss of ESSER.

entry.title: Outside money share
entry.summary: The general fund paid 81.5% of school spending in FY2009 and 89.9% in FY2025; grants and other funds the rest.

entry.title: Lines cut to zero
entry.summary: 93 of 132 school lines cut to zero were funded again later; the 39 that never were carried $181,180.

entry.title: History courses
entry.summary: 60.4% of Lunenburg High took a history course in SY2023 to SY2025, against 75.8% in SY2017 to SY2019.

entry.title: High school sections
entry.summary: Lunenburg High ran 247 course sections in SY2025 against 225 in SY2017, with 438 students against 435.

entry.title: Grant endings
entry.summary: 42.2% of the grant money that ran out in FY2025 was replaced from the general fund; the rest was not.

entry.title: Cuts against state counts
entry.summary: Of 60 adopted school cuts, 48 name a job no series counts; of the other 12, the state’s count fell with 6.

entry.title: Computer science
entry.summary: In 11 school years holding grades 9–12, Lunenburg High recorded 1 computer science section.

entry.title: AP subjects
entry.summary: 117 of 154 AP exams in SY2025 were English or history; science and math were 31.

entry.title: AP scores
entry.summary: 88.3% of AP tests scored 3 or better in SY2025, the highest of 19 years; the lowest was 62.1% in SY2009.

entry.title: AP participation
entry.summary: 89 students sat at least one AP exam in SY2025, 154 sittings between them; the count peaked at 122 in SY2018.

entry.title: Announced cuts
entry.summary: The district named 158 reductions in 9 budget documents across 5 cycles; none records what became of a post.

entry.title: Programs and cuts
entry.summary: Lunenburg High ran more classes in SY2025 than in SY2017, but a smaller share takes a language or history. Most announced cuts cannot be checked against any published count, and most budget lines cut to zero came back.

entry.title: Youth league payments
entry.summary: One league’s field payments are on record: $39,073.50 across 7 receipts, FY2024 to FY2026.

entry.title: School field upkeep
entry.summary: The district says it pays to mow its grass fields from the fund the field rent goes into.

entry.title: School facilities fund
entry.summary: The schools’ rental fund rose $62,231 in FY2025, more than its receipts in any year FY2011–FY2023.

entry.title: Registration sales
entry.summary: The registration system recorded $47,784 in FY2025, and non-residents paid 50% of it.

entry.title: Parks spending
entry.summary: By June, before the close, Parks had paid $113,350 of a $140,759 FY2026 budget; $23,141 was not yet used.

entry.title: Parks budget
entry.summary: The Parks budget voted for FY2026 was $134,434, against $64,908 in FY2010.

entry.title: Park revolving fund
entry.summary: The parks’ fee fund held $84,818 at 31 March 2026; it ended FY2015 and FY2016 at zero.

entry.title: Smaller parks funds
entry.summary: The Park Gift Fund took in $22,887 in FY2011 and stood at $752 from FY2016 to FY2025.

entry.title: Grounds maintenance bid
entry.summary: A contractor bid $44,590 for one year of grounds work at six parks, from 1 July 2024.

entry.title: Artificial turf fund
entry.summary: The Artificial Turf fund took in $45,000 in FY2026 and held $69,390 at 31 March 2026.

entry.title: Parks department
entry.summary: Town Meeting voted the Parks department $134,434 for FY2026. Beside it, a fee fund held $84,818 at 31 March 2026, and rent for school fields goes to a school fund. Neither fund is part of the vote.

entry.title: Monty Tech enrolment
entry.summary: Monty Tech enrolled 1,403 pupils in FY2026 from 18 member towns; 97 were Lunenburg residents.

entry.title: Monty Tech assessment
entry.summary: Lunenburg’s FY2026 Monty Tech bill was $1,334,521; 95.2% of it is a minimum the state sets.

entry.title: Years in the home
entry.summary: 1,799 ± 297 owner households moved in before 2010, about half; the median owner moved in in 2010.

entry.title: Population and households
entry.summary: About 11,804 residents in 4,529 households, on a sample; both grew by more than the survey’s margin.

entry.title: Bill against neighbours
entry.summary: At $7,444, the average bill is 6th of 11 nearby towns and 145 of 351 statewide.

entry.title: Residents by age
entry.summary: 1,979 ± 309 residents are 65 or over, 16.8% of the town; 2,736 ± 429 are under 18. Both are sample estimates.

entry.title: Owners and renters
entry.summary: 81.3% of occupied homes are owner-occupied, 3,682 ± 321 households, on a sample estimate.

entry.title: New growth
entry.summary: New growth added $518,650 to the FY2026 levy limit, 1.64% of the prior limit, on top of Proposition 2½.

entry.title: Income by age
entry.summary: A household headed by someone 65 or over has a median income of $72,935, 56.5% of a 45-to-64 household’s.

entry.title: Households with children
entry.summary: 1,477 ± 198 of 4,529 households have a child under 18, about a third; how many use the schools is unpublished.

entry.title: Household income
entry.summary: Median household income is $109,753 ± $12,275 on a sample, ranking 167 of 350 Massachusetts municipalities.

entry.title: Homes and enrolment
entry.summary: 773 more single-family homes since FY1994; enrolment is 321 below its FY2001 peak.

entry.title: Commercial share
entry.summary: Business property is 8.7% of the FY2026 tax base, against 10.6% in FY2002 and 7.3% in FY2023.

entry.title: Business building pace
entry.summary: Non-residential new growth averaged $19,421,113 a year in FY2024–FY2026, 3.3 times the pace before it.

entry.title: Bill by deed year
entry.summary: A home last deeded before 1986 would pay a median $5,992 before exemptions; one deeded since 2021, $6,890.

entry.title: Average tax bill
entry.summary: The average single-family bill was $7,444 in FY2026, up 47.7% in ten years while the tax rate fell 26.6%.

entry.title: Homes, taxes, growth
entry.summary: About 11,804 residents live in 4,529 households, 81.3% owner-occupied, on a Census sample. The average single-family bill was $7,444 in FY2026, and the town has 773 more single-family homes than in FY1994 while enrolment fell.

entry.title: School health insurance
entry.summary: Two school accounts hold $5,222,731 for FY2026; $1,521,536 of it sits outside the school budget.

entry.title: Retiree health accounts
entry.summary: School retiree health went from $1,119,925 in FY2022 to $1,521,536 in FY2026, 8.0% a year.

entry.title: PEC agreement
entry.summary: The town pays 75% of active premiums under a PEC agreement that runs to 30 June 2029.

entry.title: Towns compared
entry.summary: On the state’s figure, which added Medicare and life in FY2024, spending grew 6.84% a year from FY2015.

entry.title: State-reported spending
entry.summary: The state’s figure for Lunenburg counted Medicare and life insurance in FY2024, and in no year before.

entry.title: Plans and premiums
entry.summary: Premiums rose 5.38% from 1 July 2026; a Blue Care Elect family plan is $3,662.52 a month, the town paying 75%.

entry.title: Options under the law
entry.summary: Chapter 32B leaves the town 7 routes and bars 4; the PEC agreement holds 3 of them until 30 June 2029.

entry.title: Insurance department
entry.summary: The town’s insurance department grew 4.3% a year, FY2011 to FY2026, against a 2.5% levy cap.

entry.title: Growth over time
entry.summary: Filed spending rose 15.4% in FY2023, the median town 5.6%; FY2024’s figure counts more accounts.

entry.title: District health line
entry.summary: The district’s adopted health line rose from $2,633,912 in FY2018 to $3,701,195 in FY2026, 4.3% a year.

entry.title: Health insurance costs
entry.summary: The town budgeted $3,713,520 for its insurance department in FY2026, and the schools $3,701,195 on their own health line. The department grew 4.3% a year from FY2011, against a 2.5% levy cap.

entry.title: School choice flows
entry.summary: 58 residents left under school choice in FY2026 and 11 arrived; arrivals were 44 in FY2014.

entry.title: Nearby district enrolment
entry.summary: Lunenburg’s enrolment fell 14.0% from FY2008 to FY2026; 3 of 4 nearby districts fell further.

entry.title: Leaving and arriving
entry.summary: DESE’s rates imply about 90 children leave each year; enrolment fell 171 in 17 years.

entry.title: High-needs students
entry.summary: English learners went from 3 to 70; low income was measured three ways and is not one series.

entry.title: Grade-to-grade loss
entry.summary: On average 20.5% of eighth graders do not return for grade 9; other grades lose 3.0% to 6.4%.

entry.title: Grade 8 loss trend
entry.summary: The latest grade 8 rate, 27.7%, is the second-highest of 17 years, inside a range the town has always been in.

entry.title: Enrolment by year
entry.summary: 1,568 children in FY2026: 321 fewer than the FY2001 peak, and close to where the count has sat since FY2015.

entry.title: Enrolment by grade band
entry.summary: Grades 9–12 lost 30.0% of their children from FY2008 to FY2026; pre-K to grade 5 lost 5.8%.

entry.title: Departure scenario
entry.summary: A scenario on assumed rates: 78 students choosing out would take $401,700 from the town in year one.

entry.title: Children schooled elsewhere
entry.summary: 177 resident children were in other public districts in FY2026, against 186 in FY2014; the mix changed.

entry.title: Students and schools
entry.summary: 1,568 children were in Lunenburg’s schools in FY2026, near where the count has sat since FY2015. Another 177 residents were schooled in other public districts, 97 of them at Monty Tech.

entry.title: Voted budget total
entry.summary: The voted total was $44,024,349 for FY2025 and $49,374,465 for FY2026, a 12.2% rise.

entry.title: Town staff counts
entry.summary: 8 town departments print a staff count, in 7 different forms that cannot be added up.

entry.title: Trash and recycling
entry.summary: Trash and recycling grew 22.6% a year, the fastest of the twelve, from $312,634 to $469,775.

entry.title: Smaller departments
entry.summary: Veterans and elder services, health, and central purchasing are 1.2% of the budget together.

entry.title: Schools in the omnibus
entry.summary: The schools are 57.1% of the voted budget and grew 3.6% a year, FY2023 to FY2025.

entry.title: Public works
entry.summary: Public works grew 2.9% a year, close to the cap; one line rose more than the whole group.

entry.title: Police, fire and inspectors
entry.summary: Police, fire and the inspectors were voted $4,643,717 for FY2025, 10.5% of the budget.

entry.title: Library budget
entry.summary: The library was voted $583,890 for FY2025, 1.3% of the budget, growing 8.8% a year.

entry.title: Budgets without headcounts
entry.summary: 6 of the 12 budget groups have a published staff count behind them; one department with a budget has none.

entry.title: General government
entry.summary: The town’s own administration grew 10.2% a year, $168,340 past the cap in dollars, third of the twelve.

entry.title: Facilities and grounds
entry.summary: Facilities and grounds were voted $1,022,711 for FY2025 and grew 7.5% a year.

entry.title: Employee benefits
entry.summary: Employee benefits grew 12.7% a year, the most dollars past the cap of any group; group health is 71% of it.

entry.title: Debt service
entry.summary: Debt service fell from $4,497,723 to $2,941,322, FY2023 to FY2025, the only one of the twelve groups to fall.

entry.title: Budget by department
entry.summary: Schools are 57.1% of the $44,024,349 Town Meeting voted for FY2025; the next three groups together are 27.0%.

entry.title: Growth above the cap
entry.summary: Ranked by dollars above the 2.5% levy cap, employee benefits push the budget hardest, then the schools.

entry.title: Town departments
entry.summary: Town Meeting voted $44,024,349 across twelve groups for FY2025; the schools are 57.1%. Ranked by dollars past the 2.5% levy cap, employee benefits push the budget hardest, then the schools.

entry.title: Teacher contract
entry.summary: The teachers’ agreement ends 30 June 2027; each half point on the next moves the FY2028 gap $66,942 (ours).

entry.title: School user fees
entry.summary: At their limits, bus and activity fees would add $187,990 by our estimate: 20.2% of the FY2028 gap.

entry.title: Salary line and staffing
entry.summary: Held to 2.5% while pay rises 4.0%, the salary line loses 2.2 positions a year, by our arithmetic.

entry.title: Townwide or school-only
entry.summary: Of the $2,400,000 Tier 1 question, $1,600,000 was for the schools; the May 2024 one named only the schools.

entry.title: Override history
entry.summary: The state records 10 Lunenburg override questions since 1989; 4 passed, the last $948,136 in May 2024.

entry.title: Override duration
entry.summary: A school-only override that held five years would be $3,414,456 by our arithmetic; ten years, $7,442,839.

entry.title: The FY2027 override
entry.summary: Both FY2027 override questions failed on 16 May 2026: $2,400,000 by 899 to 1,748, $3,300,000 by 766 to 1,883.

entry.title: FY2027 cut size
entry.summary: The workbook puts the adopted FY2027 school budget $761,001 below Level Service; the addendum states $868,918.

entry.title: Extracurricular cuts
entry.summary: Cutting every extra still funded saves $376,207 by our grouping, 40.3% of the FY2028 gap.

entry.title: Classroom positions
entry.summary: At $89,096 a position (ours), the FY2028 gap is 10.5 positions; FY2027 already cut 4 classroom teachers.

entry.title: Closing the gap
entry.summary: Against a projected FY2028 gap of $932,664 (ours), each option has a size and a payer: an override, fees, cuts to programmes or positions, reserves, or the next teachers’ settlement.

entry.title: Seats changing hands
entry.summary: Across 37 bodies of three or more seats, the median sees 32% of its seats change hands a year.

entry.title: Board sizes
entry.summary: The FY2025 listing prints 182 holders under 60 headings; the Council on Aging is largest, with 11.

entry.title: Seats filled
entry.summary: The FY2025 listing prints 101 names against 116 seats its boards state, 87%; FY2020 read 107%.

entry.title: Meeting recordings
entry.summary: 1,173 of 1,935 meetings, FY2023 to FY2026, have a town video matched; 10 of 30 ranked boards have none.

entry.title: Open seats
entry.summary: The FY2025 annual report prints 18 seats empty under 12 headings: 15 appointed, 3 elected.

entry.title: Minutes posted
entry.summary: On the town’s Agenda Center, 1,307 of 1,935 board meetings from FY2023 to FY2026 have minutes listed, 68%.

entry.title: Minutes by year
entry.summary: All boards together list minutes for 63% to 71% of meetings a year; the School Committee, 0 of 40 in FY2023.

entry.title: Member tenure
entry.summary: Of 703 people printed in the town’s listings from FY2016 to FY2025, 19 appear in all 10.

entry.title: Boards and committees
entry.summary: Across every board, 68% of FY2023 to FY2026 meetings have minutes listed on the town’s site. In FY2025, 87% of the seats the boards state had a name printed, and the median body changes 32% of its seats a year.

entry.title: State reimbursement
entry.summary: The state repays 5.5% of what the town spends on buses, all of it for special education.

entry.title: Special education transportation
entry.summary: The fastest-growing bus line: 10.1% a year, and $67,555 past its FY2026 budget.

entry.title: FY2027 bus budget
entry.summary: School-day buses rise 11.2% in FY2027; the total shows 2.4% because athletic buses were cut.

entry.title: FY2027 athletic bus cut
entry.summary: FY2027 cut athletic buses from the town budget, then put $60,000 back, most on the fee fund.

entry.title: Dee Bus contract
entry.summary: Regular routes cost exactly the contract price, which is fixed through FY2028.

entry.title: Bus fee
entry.summary: The new bus fee did not lower what the school budget paid for buses in FY2026.

entry.title: Bus cost by sport
entry.summary: Track costs most on the district’s sheet: $13,864 in FY2024, ahead of the next sport’s $9,078.

entry.title: Away trips by sport
entry.summary: The posted schedules list 240 away games in FY2026, about 176 bus trips by our estimate.

entry.title: Athletic bus funding
entry.summary: From FY2025, athletic buses moved from player fees to the town budget, mostly taxes.

entry.title: School bus costs
entry.summary: Buses are getting more expensive, in special education and in the regular-route contract. The state repays only a slice of special education busing. The athletic line rose because the district moved that cost from player fees to the town budget, mostly taxes.

entry.title: Who may spend it
entry.summary: Only the general fund, $3,147,179 of $9,061,421, may go to any lawful use, by a two-thirds vote.

entry.title: Stabilization withdrawals
entry.summary: The record shows $317,392 taken from stabilization funds in 9 votes, none from the general fund.

entry.title: Stabilization deposits
entry.summary: Town Meeting put $350,000 into the two town funds in May 2024, and passed over both articles in May 2025.

entry.title: Stabilization fund balances
entry.summary: The town’s ledger files $9,061,421 under its nine stabilization accounts, at the start of FY2026.

entry.title: Reserves against the gap
entry.summary: Spent on the school gap, the general fund covers FY2028 and FY2029 and runs out in FY2030, by our arithmetic.

entry.title: General stabilization fund
entry.summary: The general fund’s cash rose every year from FY2012 to FY2025, to $3,147,179.

entry.title: Stabilization funds
entry.summary: The town holds $9,061,421 in nine stabilization accounts as of 1 July 2025. Only the general fund’s $3,147,179 may be spent on anything lawful.

entry.title: Tuition budget
entry.summary: FY2027 budgets out-of-district tuition at $700,142, $591,151 below FY2026, a 46% cut.

entry.title: Students with an IEP
entry.summary: 258 Lunenburg children had a special education plan in FY2026, 16.3% of those enrolled.

entry.title: Special education overruns
entry.summary: A special education line ran over its vote in 13 of 17 years; the worst, FY2013, by $223,774.

entry.title: Out-of-district tuition
entry.summary: $1,205,949 went to out-of-district tuition in FY2025; 39.3% of it was paid outside the general fund.

entry.title: Out-of-district placements
entry.summary: The town counted 10 children placed out of district in FY2025, against 30 in FY2015.

entry.title: In-district special education
entry.summary: The paraprofessional budget line grew 12.78% a year over 10 budgets; the state’s FTE fell 63.3%.

entry.title: Hiring versus placing
entry.summary: Placements fell while in-district budgets rose; nothing published shows one caused the other.

entry.title: Cost per placement
entry.summary: No published document says what one out-of-district placement costs.

entry.title: Class size limits
entry.summary: A separate special education group may hold 8 students to one educator, or 12 with an aide.

entry.title: Circuit breaker account
entry.summary: The account closed FY2026 at $281,806, down from $482,004 at the close of FY2020.

entry.title: Circuit breaker
entry.summary: The one state payment that moves when a child is placed: part of the cost, a year late, already in the vote.

entry.title: Special education costs
entry.summary: Out-of-district tuition was $1,205,949 in FY2025, and 39.3% of it was paid outside the general fund. The state repaid $579,142 in FY2026 through the circuit breaker, a year after the costs.

entry.title: Tuition at year end
entry.summary: FY2027 budgets $700,142 for the two tuition lines on which FY2026 spent $1,202,771.

entry.title: Town unspent balance
entry.summary: In June, before the close, town departments stood $858,462 under a $27,647,670 budget.

entry.title: Surplus by category
entry.summary: Accounts under budget left $1,683,552 and accounts over used $1,201,434 of it; the net is $482,118.

entry.title: Snow and Reserve Fund
entry.summary: Snow removal paid $1,038,092 against $355,571 voted; the $185,000 Reserve Fund paid nothing.

entry.title: Year-end transfers
entry.summary: Transfers moved $394,929 into school accounts and $309,839 out; the department ended $85,090 up, net.

entry.title: School retiree insurance
entry.summary: An account named for school retiree health paid $1,262,376 from the town’s insurance department.

entry.title: Psychologist line
entry.summary: One of four school psychologist accounts, $98,784 budgeted, paid nothing in FY2026.

entry.title: Paraprofessional overrun
entry.summary: Paraprofessional accounts ran $208,082 over in FY2026; $99,064 of it was paid against no budget.

entry.title: FY2026 year end
entry.summary: The school general fund ended FY2026 with $482,118 unspent, 1.8% of its budget, counting orders still owed. Counted the same way, FY2025 left $554,945. Town departments stood $858,462 under in June.

entry.title: Free cash sources
entry.summary: Two thirds of the free cash identified in July 2025, $2,457,761, was money appropriated and not spent.

entry.title: Free cash for schools
entry.summary: Kept above the 5% floor, $794,872 could be redirected, $137,792 short of the FY2028 gap (our arithmetic).

entry.title: Free cash guideline
entry.summary: Free cash is 6.65% of the budget, inside the 5% to 7% the Town cites; 7 of the last 10 years fell short.

entry.title: Free cash balance
entry.summary: The state certified $3,354,370 of free cash as of 1 July 2025, the most in any year the Town’s records list.

entry.title: Free cash and capital
entry.summary: Free cash paid $655,424 of the $1,225,000 FY2026 capital programme; FY2027 plans $991,627 of $1,830,203.

entry.title: Town budget and fee fund
entry.summary: The fee fund paid 45.8% of athletics spending in FY2024 and 5.7% in FY2025, on the town’s books.

entry.title: Total athletics cost
entry.summary: No document states one total: three sheets give $185,356 to $349,145 for the same teams in FY2024.

entry.title: Spending by category
entry.summary: Coaches and buses cost most on the district’s sheet; the town’s officials account held $0 in FY2026.

entry.title: Participation
entry.summary: The district counted 649 sport participations in FY2026, against 675 in FY2024.

entry.title: FY2026 athletics underspend
entry.summary: Athletics closed FY2026 with $55,300 of its $518,334 town budget unspent, on the town’s ledger.

entry.title: Cost per sport
entry.summary: Not one of 25 teams carries the same FY2024 cost in all three district sheets.

entry.title: Athletic fee
entry.summary: The high school fee for a first child, a season, went from $250 in FY2025 to $325 in FY2026.

entry.title: Athletics costs
entry.summary: Athletics is paid from two pots, the town budget and a fee fund. The town’s ledger shows $463,034 spent in FY2026 and the fee fund $146,911; the district’s own sheets disagree on what each team costs, by a multiple.

entry.title: The annual town reports
entry.summary: Every annual town report, 1959 to FY2025, each one downloadable with the sha256 of the bytes we hold — and what we read out of them, by category. Says plainly which pages tie to a total the page itself prints, and why the rest cannot be checked from the page.

entry.title: Towns like us: what they pay, what they spend
entry.summary: How Lunenburg compares with the towns it borders, the peers this project chose, and the towns most like it across the whole state, on what a town is and what it does — with a map of every town in Massachusetts.

entry.summary: What the town is deciding now

entry.title: The School Committee’s finances — every fund and line it owns
entry.summary: The School Committee’s finances, every line: the appropriation, its revolving funds, grants, gifts and trusts, with what each held at 31 March 2026 and what it has done since FY2011 — the first of a page per board and department, from a registry of every accounting measure the town prints.

entry.title: The budget feed — every board, everything about money
entry.summary: What every board is doing to prepare for Town Meeting: the omnibus budget, the school budget above all, and the warrant. What is coming, where this cycle stands, what was said most recently, what was posted. Not every mention of money — the budget being built, and what will land on the warrant.

entry.title: The boards — each one, in one place
entry.summary: Every board and committee the town posts for, one page each: what is coming, what happened, every vote we have minutes for, where the board’s time goes, and when budget season has fallen on its agendas in past years.

entry.title: This week in town — meetings coming up, minutes and recordings just posted
entry.summary: Meetings coming up for the Select Board, Finance Committee and School Committee with what is on each agenda, minutes just posted, recordings just published, and what happened at the last recorded meetings. Refreshed daily.

entry.title: Meeting minutes — written from the recordings
entry.summary: Our minutes of recorded meetings, written from the captions: votes, transfers, budget items, decisions and public comment, every item linked to the video at that second, and checked against the town’s minutes where they exist.

entry.title: The blog — one finding at a time, in two minutes
entry.summary: Every finding this project has published as a post: the figures, what it means for a resident, a Finance Committee member and a School Committee member, and the links to the report underneath it. About two minutes each.

entry.title: What a family actually pays
entry.summary: Every school fee a Lunenburg household can be charged, priced for one to four children, and the three places the published record runs out.

entry.title: If students leave — what school choice would cost
entry.summary: What it would cost the town if more children left under school choice — a scenario with dials, priced against DESE’s own counts.

entry.title: What you can ask this archive
entry.summary: Every question this archive can answer, in plain English and without a line of SQL. The list a resident should start from: pick the question you actually have and follow it to the figure and the document behind it.

entry.title: A hundred questions this archive can answer
entry.summary: The same questions with the query that answers each one, run against the database on every build — so none of them is a claim about what this data can do. If one stops answering, the build fails.

entry.title: Connecting the school budget to the Town's books
entry.summary: What can be followed from the school budget to the town’s books, and where it stops. Two levels join, the third cannot, and the format a report arrives in decides which.
